job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Bianca Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in accounts payable at a freight company in Perth, paying trucking and shipping invoices and chasing the ones that don't match. I did a finance degree, passed, no internships, and I've been there four months. I share a unit with a friend from uni, Mia. My parents run a Cantonese restaurant, so Sundays I'm back there doing the family lunch, and sometimes the till. Evenings I do a bit of baking for church bake sales and scroll property listings I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I expected. I use an AI helper now and then for Excel formulas, and it's fine. I'd tell my parents it's overblown, and they'd say good, because they've seen plenty of fashions come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly secure. Freight never stops, and invoices need someone to handle odd cases. I'd still be doing the same job in five years, a bit faster. That's a decent life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, save 450 a month for a deposit, and finish the accounting certificate my company will pay for. I'd keep helping at the restaurant on Sundays. And I'd keep an eye on flats, even if I can't buy yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nice and boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the deposit. Even with about ten thousand saved, flats here cost many times that. And my parents' restaurant has had a hard year with food prices, so I wonder if I'll end up helping them with money instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame high taxes and red tape on small businesses, and a housing market that makes it hard for people who work hard. Not AI.

I'd use the helper for Excel formulas now and then.
think: I'd feel **fairly secure**: freight never stops and odd invoices need a person.
I'd still be doing the same job in five years, and that's a **decent life**.
do: Save **450 a month** for a deposit and finish the company-paid accounting certificate.
Keep helping at the **restaurant** on Sundays.

fieldNote: Content with her job, but the **deposit** and the restaurant's costs keep her mood from being fully calm.
Steady adaptability: tries a tool, sees it's fine.
Blames **taxes, red tape** and housing, in a free-market way.

steps.text: Save 450 a month toward a flat deposit
Finish the accounting certificate the company pays for
Keep working the Sunday lunch at my parents' restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fair enough, businesses will use what's cheaper. I'd tell my manager that we should test it on a small batch of invoices before trusting it. At home I'd say, learn it before it learns you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, accounts payable is a target. Matching invoices to orders is checking, and software is good at that. Our team is four people and I'm the newest. If they trim, I'm first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI daily for matching and flagging, and be the one who knows how to catch its errors. I'd ask to move to supplier relations, where I'm calling people, or into the finance planning team. I'd keep the certificate going, and cut my spending a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I tell myself I've got time and then I remember I've been there four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The matching, definitely, the part where I compare an invoice to a purchase order. I do about sixty of those a day. My manager would notice because we'd stop needing the overtime we pay in quarter-end week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to say plainly how many roles are changing, and to pay for training in the new system. I'd rather hear the truth than a pep talk.

say: I'd say businesses will use what's **cheaper**, so test it on a small batch first.
I'd say at home, learn it before it learns you.
think: Accounts payable is a **target**, and matching invoices to orders is exactly checking.
Our team is four and I'm the **newest**, so I'd be first to go.
do: Use AI daily for matching and flagging and become the one who **catches its errors**.
Ask to move to **supplier relations** or the planning team.
feel: **Anxious**; I've only been there four months.
S1.quote: Our team is four people and I'm the newest. If they trim, I'm first.
fieldNote: Her own role is **plainly exposed**, and she sees it.
Her response is practical: use tools, move toward people-facing work.
Wants an employer that tells the **truth**, not a pep talk.

steps.text: Use AI daily to match invoices and flag mismatches
Ask to move to supplier relations
Keep going with the company-paid certificate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and I hope the people in charge are paying attention. I'd say that families and businesses will carry a lot of this, so we need to look after one another. I'd say it to my parents first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm really worried. Two years is no time. I've just started, my work is entirely paperwork, and my parents' restaurant can't pay me either. If I lose my job, I'm the one who needs help, not the one who gives it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd tighten up. Cancel subscriptions, cook at home, and push my savings from ten up to fifteen thousand. I'd learn the AI tools hard, nights and weekends. Then I'd ask my uncle, who has a small import business, if I could do his books and maybe learn the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed. My chest gets tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my parents to talk through the restaurant's money. Then I'd ask my manager how safe my job is. I'd talk to Mia about moving to a cheaper place together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm saving and have a plan, and I'd keep the fear to myself, since she carries enough already. I'd tell my dad I might need to help at the restaurant more, and he'd pretend not to be glad.

say: I'd say it's **frightening**, and families and businesses will carry a lot, so we must look after one another.
I'd say it to my parents first.
think: Two years is **no time**: I've just started and my work is all paperwork.
If I lose my job, I'm the one who needs **help**.
do: Cancel subscriptions and push savings toward **fifteen thousand**.
Learn the **AI tools** on nights and weekends and ask my uncle about his books.
feel: **Anxious**, close to alarmed, with a tight chest.
S2.quote: If I lose my job, I'm the one who needs help, not the one who gives it.
fieldNote: Strong sense of **family duty** makes the stakes bigger.

steps.text: Cancel subscriptions and cook at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same thing, a bit kinder. I'd say five years is enough for firms and families to adjust if they start now. I'd say to my parents that the restaurant should think about how it'll compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a lot more settled. Five years is long enough to qualify properly and move into something less exposed. I'd be twenty-seven. I wouldn't be afraid of a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd finish the certificate, move into planning, use AI openly, and keep saving 500 a month. I'd help my parents think about ordering and bookings, using the tools. I'd stay in the unit with Mia to keep costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's a bit like a long exam run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd probably still try to buy a small flat, but a smaller one, further out. In two years I wouldn't touch a mortgage. I wouldn't know if I'd be earning when the payments started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd split it: some into the deposit, some into the restaurant's online booking system, which my parents never got around to. I think it would pay for itself, and it would keep them going.

I'd tell my parents the restaurant should think about how it'll compete.
think: I'm a lot **more settled**: five years is long enough to qualify and move to something less exposed.
I wouldn't be **afraid** of a plan.

fieldNote: Time lets her keep the **flat** dream alive, shrunk but real.

steps.text: Finish the certificate and move into the planning team

Use AI openly at work and check every result

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people don't waste it. I'd say schools and firms should start teaching the trades and the tools now, and I'd tell younger cousins to pick something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. At thirty-two I'd hope to have a flat, maybe a partner, and a job that's mostly judgement. Even if AI did all my current work, I'd have had time to turn myself into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, finish the certificate, work up to a finance manager, and save for a deposit. I'd keep learning the tools one step ahead of the team. And I'd keep my Sunday lunches, because they keep me grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build something with my family, maybe turn the restaurant into several, using the tools to run them lean. In two years I'd be thinking only about survival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not exactly. I'd like to run something, maybe be my own boss. I'd still want the family around me while I did it.

I'd tell my younger cousins to pick something with people in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I've no cushion beyond about ten thousand, no experience, and my family leans on me. What would help is time, a plan for retraining, and my company being honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people say my generation wants everything easy. I'd say I want things fair, a job, a flat, a family. That's old-fashioned, really.

headlineQuote: I want things fair, a job, a flat, a family. That's old-fashioned, really.
portrait: Bianca is 22, an accounts payable clerk at a Perth freight company, four months into her first job.
She uses AI now and then for Excel, picks up tools once others have, and checks results carefully.
Her outlook is traditional and pro-market: family business, church bake sales, and little patience for red tape and high taxes.
With ten thousand saved and a family restaurant behind her, she is **uneasy** in slow worlds, anxious when time is short.
Given time she plans a smaller flat, a finance manager role and perhaps expanding her parents' restaurant.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries her most, with a thin cushion, little experience and a family leaning on her.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **time**, a retraining plan and an honest employer.
